entries.5e5c72019a29a4c3933ec491dd1dea2eacb33995: <div sID="gen31618" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="12" osisID="2Cor.12" sID="2Cor.12"/> <div eID="gen31618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31619" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31620" type="x-p"/> In this chapter the apostle proceeds in maintaining the honour of his apostleship. He magnified his office when there were those who vilified it. What he says in his own praise was only in his own justification and the necessary defence of the honour of his ministry, the preservation of which was necessary to its success. First, He makes mention of the favour God had shown him, the honour done him, the methods God took to keep him humble, and the use he made of this dispensation, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.1-2Cor.12.10">ver. 1-10</reference>. Then he addresses himself to the Corinthians, blaming them for what was faulty among them, and giving a large account of his behaviour and kind intentions towards them, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.11-2Cor.12.21">ver. 11, to the end</reference>.
entries.b00b151109fbad2c33b3cba21b4171619b86a929: <div eID="gen31620" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31619" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Apostle's Rapture. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31621" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> It is not expedient for me doubtless to glory. I will come to visions and revelations of the Lord. <hi type="super">2</hi> I knew a man in Christ above fourteen years ago, (whether in the body, I cannot tell; or whether out of the body, I cannot tell: God knoweth;) such an one caught up to the third heaven. <hi type="super">3</hi> And I knew such a man, (whether in the body, or out of the body, I cannot tell: God knoweth;) <hi type="super">4</hi> How that he was caught up into paradise, and heard unspeakable words, which it is not lawful for a man to utter. <hi type="super">5</hi> Of such an one will I glory: yet of myself I will not glory, but in mine infirmities. <hi type="super">6</hi> For though I would desire to glory, I shall not be a fool; for I will say the truth: but <hi type="italic">now</hi> I forbear, lest any man should think of me above that which he seeth me <hi type="italic">to be,</hi> or <hi type="italic">that</hi> he heareth of me. <hi type="super">7</hi> And lest I should be exalted above measure through the abundance of the revelations, there was given to me a thorn in the flesh, the messenger of Satan to buffet me, lest I should be exalted above measure. <hi type="super">8</hi> For this thing I besought the Lord thrice, that it might depart from me. <hi type="super">9</hi> And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me. <hi type="super">10</hi> Therefore I take pleasure in infirmities, in reproaches, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ's sake: for when I am weak, then am I strong. <div eID="gen31621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31622" type="x-p"/> Here we may observe, <div eID="gen31622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31623" type="x-p"/> I. The narrative the apostle gives of the favours God had shown him, and the honour he had done him; for doubtless he himself is the man in Christ of whom he speaks. Concerning this we may take notice, 1. Of the honour itself which was done to the apostle: he was <hi type="italic">caught up into the third heaven,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.2">v. 2</reference>. When this was we cannot say, whether it was during those three days that he lay without sight at his conversion or at some other time afterwards, much less can we pretend to say <hi type="italic">how</hi> this was, whether by a separation of his soul from his body or by an extraordinary transport in the depth of contemplation. It would be presumption for us to determine, if not also to enquire into, this matter, seeing the apostle himself says, <hi type="italic">Whether in the body or out of the body, I cannot tell.</hi> It was certainly a very extraordinary honour done him: in some sense he was caught up into the <hi type="italic">third heaven,</hi> the heaven of the blessed, above the a&#235;rial heaven, in which the fowls fly, above the starry heaven, which is adorned with those glorious orbs: it was into the third heaven, where God most eminently manifests his glory. We are not capable of knowing all, nor is it fit we should know very much, of the particulars of that glorious place and state; it is our duty and interest to give diligence to make sure to ourselves a mansion there; and, if that be cleared up to us, then we should long to be removed thither, to abide there for ever. This third heaven is called paradise (<reference osisRef="2Cor.12.4">v. 4</reference>), in allusion to the earthly paradise out of which Adam was driven for his transgression; it is called the paradise of God (<reference osisRef="Rev.2.7">Rev. ii. 7</reference>), signifying to us that by Christ we are restored to all the joys and honours we lost by sin, yea, to much better. The apostle does not mention what he saw in the third heaven or paradise, but tells us that <hi type="italic">he heard unspeakable words,</hi> such as it is not possible for a man to utter—such are the sublimity of the matter and our unacquaintedness with the language of the upper world: nor was it lawful to utter those words, because, while we are here in this world, we have a more sure word of prophecy than such visions and revelations. <reference osisRef="2Pet.1.19">2 Pet. i. 19</reference>. We read of the tongue of angels as well as men, and Paul knew as much of that as ever any man upon earth did, and yet preferred charity, that is, the sincere love of God and our neighbour. This account which the apostle gives us of his vision should check our curious desires after forbidden knowledge, and teach us to improve the revelation God has given us in his word. Paul himself, who had been in the third heaven, did not publish to the world what he had heard there, but adhered to the doctrine of Christ: on this foundation the church is built, and on this we must build our faith and hope. 2. The modest and humble manner in which the apostle mentions this matter is observable. One would be apt to think that one who had had such visions and revelations as these would have boasted greatly of them; but, says he, <hi type="italic">It is not expedient for me doubtless to glory,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.1">v. 1</reference>. He therefore did not mention this immediately, nor till <hi type="italic">above fourteen years</hi> after, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.2">v. 2</reference>. And then it is not without some reluctancy, as a thing which in a manner he was forced to by the necessity of the case. Again, he speaks of himself in the third person, and does not say, I am the man who was thus honoured above other men. Again, his humility appears by the check he seems to put upon himself (<reference osisRef="2Cor.12.6">v. 6</reference>), which plainly shows that he delighted not to dwell upon this theme. Thus was he, who was not behind the chief of the apostles in dignity, very eminent for his humility. Note, It is an excellent thing to have a lowly spirit in the midst of high advancements; and those who abase themselves shall be exalted. <div eID="gen31623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31624" type="x-p"/> II. The apostle gives an account of the methods God took to keep him humble, and to prevent his <hi type="italic">being lifted up above measure;</hi> and this he speaks of to balance the account that was given before of the visions and revelations he had had. Note, When God's people communicate their experiences, let them always remember to take notice of what God has done to keep them humble, as well as what he has done in favour to them and for their advancement. Here observe, <div eID="gen31624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31625" type="x-p"/> 1. The apostle was pained with a thorn in the flesh, and buffeted with a messenger of Satan, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.7">v. 7</reference>. We are much in the dark what this was, whether some great trouble or some great temptation. Some think it was an acute bodily pain or sickness; others think it was the indignities done him by the false apostles, and the opposition he met with from them, particularly on the account of his speech, which was contemptible. However this was, God often brings this good out of evil, that the reproaches of our enemies help to hide pride from us; and this is certain, that what the apostle calls a thorn in his flesh was for a time very grievous to him: but the thorns Christ wore for us, and with which he was crowned, sanctify and make easy all the thorns in the flesh we may at any time be afflicted with; for <hi type="italic">he suffered, being tempted, that he might be able to succour those that are tempted.</hi> Temptations to sin are most grievous thorns; they are messengers of Satan, to buffet us. Indeed it is a great grievance to a good man to be so much as tempted to sin. <div eID="gen31625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31626" type="x-p"/> 2. The design of this was to keep the apostle humble: <hi type="italic">Lest he should be exalted above measure,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.7">v. 7</reference>. Paul himself knew he <hi type="italic">had not yet attained, neither was already perfect;</hi> and yet he was in danger of being lifted up with pride. If God love us, he will hide pride from us, and keep us from being exalted above measure; and spiritual burdens are ordered, to cure spiritual pride. This thorn in the flesh is said to be a messenger of Satan, which he did not send with a good design, but on the contrary, with ill intentions, to discourage the apostle (who had been so highly favoured of God) and hinder him in his work. But God designed this for good, and he overruled it for good, and made this messenger of Satan to be so far from being a hindrance that it was a help to the apostle. <div eID="gen31626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31627" type="x-p"/> 3. The apostle prayed earnestly to God for the removal of this sore grievance. Note, Prayer is a salve for every sore, a remedy for every malady; and when we are afflicted with thorns in the flesh we should give ourselves to prayer. Therefore we are sometimes tempted that we may learn to pray. The apostle <hi type="italic">besought the Lord thrice, that it might depart from him,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.8">v. 8</reference>. Note, Though afflictions are sent for our spiritual benefit, yet we may pray to God for the removal of them: we ought indeed to desire also that they may reach the end for which they are designed. The apostle prayed earnestly, and repeated his requests; he besought the Lord <hi type="italic">thrice,</hi> that is, often. So that if an answer be not given to the first prayer, nor to the second, we must hold on, and hold out, till we receive an answer. Christ himself prayed to his Father thrice. As troubles are sent to teach us to pray, so they are continued to teach us to continue instant in prayer. <div eID="gen31627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31628" type="x-p"/> 4. We have an account of the answer given to the apostle's prayer, that, although the trouble was not removed, yet an equivalent should be granted: <hi type="italic">My grace is sufficient for thee.</hi> Note, (1.) Though God accepts the prayer of faith, yet he does not always answer it in the letter; as he sometimes grants in wrath, so he sometimes denies in love. (2.) When God does not remove our troubles and temptations, yet, if he gives us grace sufficient for us, we have no reason to complain, nor to say that he deals ill by us. It is a great comfort to us, whatever thorns in the flesh we are pained with, that God's grace is sufficient for us. Grace signifies two things:—[1.] The good-will of God towards us, and this is enough to enlighten and enliven us, sufficient to strengthen and comfort us, to support our souls and cheer up our spirits, in all afflictions and distresses. [2.] The good work of God in us, the grace we receive from the fulness that is in Christ our head; and from him there shall be communicated that which is suitable and seasonable, and sufficient for his members. Christ Jesus understands our case, and knows our need, and will proportion the remedy to our malady, and not only strengthen us, but glorify <hi type="italic">himself. His strength is made perfect in our weakness.</hi> Thus his grace is manifested and magnified; he ordains his praise out of the mouths of babes and sucklings. <div eID="gen31628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31629" type="x-p"/> III. Here is the use which the apostle makes of this dispensation: <hi type="italic">He gloried in his infirmities</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.12.9">v. 9</reference>), and took pleasure in them, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.10">v. 10</reference>. He does not mean his sinful infirmities (those we have reason to be ashamed of and grieved at), but he means his afflictions, his reproaches, necessities, persecutions, and distresses for Christ's sake, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.10">v. 10</reference>. And the reason of his glory and joy on account of these things was this—they were fair opportunities for Christ to manifest the power and sufficiency of his grace resting upon him, by which he had so much experience of the strength of divine grace that he could say, <hi type="italic">When I am weak, then am I strong.</hi> This is a Christian paradox: when we are weak in ourselves, then we are strong in the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ; when we see ourselves weak in ourselves, then we go out of ourselves to Christ, and are qualified to receive strength from him, and experience most of the supplies of divine strength and grace.
entries.d75ae1a39f9ae92de5edfe7074b35415e9d7c423: <div eID="gen31629" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Paul's Expostulations. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31630" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> I am become a fool in glorying; ye have compelled me: for I ought to have been commended of you: for in nothing am I behind the very chiefest apostles, though I be nothing. <hi type="super">12</hi> Truly the signs of an apostle were wrought among you in all patience, in signs, and wonders, and mighty deeds. 13 For what is it wherein ye were inferior to other churches, except <hi type="italic">it be</hi> that I myself was not burdensome to you? forgive me this wrong. <hi type="super">14</hi> Behold, the third time I am ready to come to you; and I will not be burdensome to you: for I seek not yours, but you: for the children ought not to lay up for the parents, but the parents for the children. <hi type="super">15</hi> And I will very gladly spend and be spent for you; though the more abundantly I love you, the less I be loved. <hi type="super">16</hi> But be it so, I did not burden you: nevertheless, being crafty, I caught you with guile. 17 Did I make a gain of you by any of them whom I sent unto you? <hi type="super">18</hi> I desired Titus, and with <hi type="italic">him</hi> I sent a brother. Did Titus make a gain of you? walked we not in the same spirit? <hi type="italic">walked we</hi> not in the same steps? <hi type="super">19</hi> Again, think ye that we excuse ourselves unto you? we speak before God in Christ: but <hi type="italic">we do</hi> all things, dearly beloved, for your edifying. <hi type="super">20</hi> For I fear, lest, when I come, I shall not find you such as I would, and <hi type="italic">that</hi> I shall be found unto you such as ye would not: lest <hi type="italic">there be</hi> debates, envyings, wraths, strifes, backbitings, whisperings, swellings, tumults: 21 <hi type="italic">And</hi> lest, when I come again, my God will humble me among you, and <hi type="italic">that</hi> I shall bewail many which have sinned already, and have not repented of the uncleanness and fornication and lasciviousness which they have committed. <div eID="gen31630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31631" type="x-p"/> In these verses the apostle addresses himself to the Corinthians two ways:— <div eID="gen31631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31632" type="x-p"/> I. He blames them for what was faulty in them; namely, that they had not stood up in his defence as they ought to have done, and so made it the more needful for him to insist so much on his own vindication. They in manner compelled him to commend himself, who <hi type="italic">ought to have been commended of them</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.11">v. 11</reference>. And had they, or some among them, not failed on their part, it would have been less needful for him to have said so much on his own behalf. He tells them further that they in particular had good reason to speak well of him, as being <hi type="italic">in nothing behind the very chief apostles,</hi> because he had given them full proof and evidence of his apostleship; for <hi type="italic">the signs of an apostle were wrought among them in all patience, in signs, and wonders, and mighty deeds.</hi> Note, 1. It is a debt we owe to good men to stand up in the defence of their reputation; and we are under special obligations to those we have received benefit by, especially spiritual benefit, to own them as instruments in God's hand of good to us, and to vindicate them when they are calumniated by others. 2. How much soever we are, or ought to be, esteemed by others, we ought always to think humbly of ourselves. See an example of this in this great apostle, who thought himself to be nothing, though in truth he was not behind the greatest apostles—so far was he from seeking praise from men, though he tells them their duty to vindicate his reputation—so far was he from applauding himself, when he was forced to insist upon his own necessary self-defence. <div eID="gen31632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31633" type="x-p"/> II. He gives a large account of his behaviour and kind intentions towards them, in which we may observe the character of a faithful minister of the gospel. 1. He was not willing to be burdensome to them, nor did he seek theirs, but them. He says (<reference osisRef="2Cor.12.13">v. 13</reference>) he had not been burdensome to them, for the time past, and tells them (<reference osisRef="2Cor.12.14">v. 14</reference>) he would not be burdensome to them for the time to come, when he should come to them. He spared their purses, and did not covet their money: <hi type="italic">I seek not yours but you.</hi> He sought not to enrich himself, but to save their souls: he did not desire to make a property of them to himself, but to gain them over to Christ, whose servant he was. Note, Those who aim at clothing themselves with the fleece of the flock, and take no care of the sheep, are hirelings, and not good shepherds. 2. He would gladly spend and be spent for them (<reference osisRef="2Cor.12.15">v. 15</reference>); that is, he was willing to take pains and to suffer loss for their good. He would spend his time, his parts, his strength, his interest, his all, to do them service; nay, so spend as to be spent, and be like a candle, which consumes itself to give light to others. 3. He did not abate in his love to them, notwithstanding their unkindness and ingratitude to him; and therefore was contented and glad to take pains with them, though <hi type="italic">the more abundantly he loved them the less he was loved,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.15">v. 15</reference>. This is applicable to other relations: if others be wanting in their duty to us it does not follow therefore that we may neglect our duty to them. 4. He was careful not only that he himself should not be burdensome, but that none he employed should. This seems to be the meaning of what we read, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.16-2Cor.12.18">v. 16-18</reference>. If it should be objected by any that though he did not himself burden them, <hi type="italic">yet, being crafty, he caught them with guile,</hi> that is, he sent those among them who pillaged them, and afterwards he shared with them in the profit: "This was not so," says the apostle; "I did not make a gain of you myself, nor by any of those whom I sent; nor did Titus, nor any others—We walked by the same spirit and in the same steps." They all agreed in this matter to do them all the good they could, without being burdensome to them, to promote the gospel among them and make it as easy to them as possible. Or, this may be read with an interrogation, as utterly disclaiming any guile in himself and others towards them. 5. He was a man who did all things for edifying, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.19">v. 19</reference>. This was his great aim and design, to do good, to lay the foundation well, and then with care and diligence to build the superstructure. 6. He would not shrink from his duty for fear of displeasing them, though he was so careful to make himself easy to them. Therefore he was resolved to be faithful in reproving sin, though he was therein <hi type="italic">found to be such as they would not,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.20">v. 20</reference>. The apostle here mentions several sins that are too commonly found among professors of religion, and are very reprovable: <hi type="italic">debates, envyings, wraths, strifes, backbitings, whisperings, swellings, tumults;</hi> and, though those who are guilty of these sins can hardly bear to be reproved for them, yet faithful ministers must not fear offending the guilty by sharp reproofs, as they are needful, in public and in private. 7. He was grieved at the apprehension that he should find scandalous sins among them not duly repented of. This, he tells them, would be the cause of great humiliation and lamentation. Note, (1.) The falls and miscarriages of professors cannot but be a humbling consideration to a good minister; and God sometimes takes this way to humble those who might be under temptation to be lifted up: <hi type="italic">I fear lest my God will humble me among you.</hi> (2.) We have reason to bewail those who sin and do not repent, to <hi type="italic">bewail many that have sinned, and have not repented,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.21">v. 21</reference>. If these have not, as yet, grace to mourn and lament their own case, their case is the more lamentable; and those who love God, and love them, should mourn for them.  <chapter eID="2Cor.12"/> <div eID="gen31633" type="x-p"/>

entries.68b69d24cadf3ccb3a1f2afef7d29cca9408dfe5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17389"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 12</title> <div sID="gen34740" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.1-2Cor.12.21">2Co 12:1-21</reference>. Revelations in Which He Might Glory: But He Rather Glories in Infirmities, as Calling Forth Christ's Power: Signs of His Apostleship: His Disinterestedness: Not That He Is Excusing Himself to Them; but He Does All for Their Good, lest He Should Find Them Not Such as He Desired, and So Should Have to Be Severe at His Coming.<div eID="gen34740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34741" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17389"/>1. He proceeds to illustrate the "glorying in infirmities" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.30">2Co 11:30</reference>). He gave one instance which might expose him to ridicule (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.33">2Co 11:33</reference>); he now gives another, but this one connected with a glorious revelation of which it was the sequel: but he dwells not on the glory done to himself, but on the infirmity which followed it, as displaying Christ's power. The oldest manuscripts read, "I MUST NEEDS boast (or glory) though it be not expedient; for I will come." The "for" gives a proof that it is "not expedient to boast": I will take the case of revelations, in which if anywhere boasting might be thought harmless. "Visions" refers to things seen: "revelations," to things heard (compare <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.15">1Sa 9:15</reference>) or revealed in any way. In "visions" their signification was not always vouchsafed; in "revelations" there was always an unveiling of truths before hidden (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.19">Da 2:19</reference>, 31). All parts of Scripture alike are matter of inspiration; but not all of revelation. There are degrees of revelation; but not of inspiration.<div eID="gen34741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34742" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of--</hi>that is, from the Lord; Christ, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.2">2Co 12:2</reference>. <div eID="gen34742" type="x-p"/>
entries.f223529aca37f99a446593f7852f018d5b0032bf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17390"/><div sID="gen34743" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17390"/>2. Translate, "I know," not "I knew."<div eID="gen34743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34744" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a man--</hi>meaning himself. But he purposely thus distinguishes between the rapt and glorified person of <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.2">2Co 12:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.4">4</reference>, and himself the infirmity-laden victim of the "thorn in the flesh" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.12.7">2Co 12:7</reference>). Such glory belonged not to him, but the weakness did. Nay, he did not even know whether he was in or out of the body when the glory was put upon him, so far was the glory from being his [Alford]. His spiritual self was his highest and truest self: the flesh with its infirmity merely his temporary self (<reference osisRef="Rom.7.25">Ro 7:25</reference>). Here, however, the latter is the prominent thought.<div eID="gen34744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34745" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in Christ--</hi>a Christian (<reference osisRef="Rom.16.7">Ro 16:7</reference>).<div eID="gen34745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34746" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">above--</hi>rather, simply "fourteen years ago." This Epistle was written A.D. 55-57. Fourteen years before will bring the vision to A.D. 41-43, the time of his second visit to Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Acts.22.17">Ac 22:17</reference>). He had long been intimate with the Corinthians, yet had never mentioned this revelation before: it was not a matter lightly to be spoken of.<div eID="gen34746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34747" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I cannot tell--</hi>rather as Greek, "I know not." If in the body, he must have been caught up bodily; if out of the body, as seems to be Paul's opinion, his spirit must have been caught up out of the body. At all events he recognizes the possibility of conscious receptivity in disembodied spirits.<div eID="gen34747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34748" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">caught up--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Acts.8.39">Ac 8:39</reference>).<div eID="gen34748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34749" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to the third heaven--</hi>even to, &c. These raptures (note the plural, "visions," "revelations," <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.1">2Co 12:1</reference>) had two degrees: first he was caught up "to the third heaven," and from thence to "Paradise" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.12.4">2Co 12:4</reference>) [Clement of Alexandria, Miscellanies, 5.427], which seems to denote an inner recess of the third heaven [Bengel] (<reference osisRef="Luke.23.43">Lu 23:43</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.2.7">Re 2:7</reference>). Paul was permitted not only to "hear" the things of Paradise, but to see also in some degree the things of the third heaven (compare "visions," <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.1">2Co 12:1</reference>). The occurrence TWICE of "whether in the body ... I know not, God knoweth," and of "lest I should be exalted above measure," marks two stages in the revelation. "Ignorance of the mode does not set aside the certain knowledge of the fact. The apostles were ignorant of many things" [Bengel]. The first heaven is that of the clouds, the air; the second, that of the stars, the sky; the third is spiritual (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.10">Ep 4:10</reference>). <div eID="gen34749" type="x-p"/>
entries.bc7f455f05d5665acaee578c7142b070f3c6eea4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17391"/><div sID="gen34750" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17391"/>3. Translate, "I know."<div eID="gen34750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34751" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">out of--</hi>Most of the oldest manuscripts read "apart from." <div eID="gen34751" type="x-p"/>
entries.701eb4ae62c312a218dff56a536640262f5ff246: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17392"/><div sID="gen34752" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17392"/><hi type="bold">4. unspeakable--</hi>not in themselves, otherwise Paul could not have heard them; but as the explanation states, "which it is not lawful ... to utter" [Alford]. They were designed for Paul's own consolation, and not for communication to others. Some heavenly words are communicable (<reference osisRef="Exod.34.6">Ex 34:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.6.3">Is 6:3</reference>). These were not so. Paul had not the power adequately to utter; nor if he had, would he have been permitted; nor would earthly men comprehend them (<reference osisRef="John.3.12">Joh 3:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.9">1Co 2:9</reference>). A man may hear and know more than he can speak. <div eID="gen34752" type="x-p"/>
entries.5c2d88329ae01a9065fbf06bdf418a92282e52ec: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17393"/><div sID="gen34753" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17393"/><hi type="bold">5. of myself--</hi>concerning myself. Self is put in the background, except in respect to his infirmities. His glorying in his other self, to which the revelations were vouchsafed, was not in order to give glory to his fleshly self, but to bring out in contrast the "infirmities" of the latter, that Christ might have all the glory. <div eID="gen34753" type="x-p"/>
entries.119150207b6afee074fd95036238a989aaecc208: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17394"/><div sID="gen34754" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17394"/><hi type="bold">6. For--</hi>Not but that I might glory as to "myself" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.12.5">2Co 12:5</reference>); "FOR if I should desire to glory, I shall not be a fool"; for I have things to glory, or boast of which are good matter for glorying of (not mere external fleshly advantages which when he gloried in [2Co 11:1-33] he termed such glorying "folly," <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.1">2Co 11:1</reference>, 16, 17).<div eID="gen34754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34755" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">think of me--</hi>Greek, "form his estimate respecting me."<div eID="gen34755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34756" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heareth of me--</hi>Greek, "heareth aught from me." Whatever haply he heareth from me in person. If on account of healing a cripple (<reference osisRef="Acts.14.12">Ac 14:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.14.13">13</reference>), and shaking off a viper (<reference osisRef="Acts.28.5">Ac 28:5</reference>), the people thought him a god, what would they have not done, if he had disclosed those revelations? [Estius]. I wish each of you to estimate me by "what he sees" my present acts and "hears" my teaching to be; not by my boasting of past revelations. They who allow themselves to be thought of more highly than is lawful, defraud themselves of the honor which is at God's disposal [Bengel] (<reference osisRef="John.5.44">Joh 5:44</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.12.43">12:43</reference>). <div eID="gen34756" type="x-p"/>
entries.32eb869640de5b5504ea7c0b86b003ff87be781c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17395"/><div sID="gen34757" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17395"/><hi type="bold">7. exalted above measure--</hi>Greek, "overmuch uplifted." How dangerous must self-exaltation be, when even the apostle required so much restraint! [Bengel].<div eID="gen34757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34758" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">abundance--</hi>Greek, "the excess"; exceeding greatness.<div eID="gen34758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34759" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">given ... me--</hi>namely, by God (<reference osisRef="Job.5.6">Job 5:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.1.29">Php 1:29</reference>).<div eID="gen34759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34760" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thorn in the flesh--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Num.33.55">Nu 33:55</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.24">Eze 28:24</reference>). Alford thinks it to be the same bodily affliction as in <reference osisRef="Gal.4.13">Ga 4:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gal.4.14">14</reference>. It certainly was something personal, affecting him individually, and not as an apostle: causing at once acute pain (as "thorn" implies) and shame ("buffet": as slaves are buffeted, <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.20">1Pe 2:20</reference>).<div eID="gen34760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34761" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">messenger of Satan--</hi>who is permitted by God to afflict His saints, as Job (<reference osisRef="Job.2.7">Job 2:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.13.16">Lu 13:16</reference>).<div eID="gen34761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34762" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to buffet me--</hi>In Greek, present: to buffet me even now continuously. After experiencing the state of the blissful angels, he is now exposed to the influence of an evil angel. The chastisement from hell follows soon upon the revelation from heaven. As his sight and hearing had been ravished with heavenly "revelations," so his touch is pained with the "thorn in the flesh." <div eID="gen34762" type="x-p"/>
entries.ef7cb337f5ca0e3211ed1784cb1636ab6a3f3594: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17396"/><div sID="gen34763" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17396"/><hi type="bold">8. For--</hi>"concerning this thing."<div eID="gen34763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34764" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thrice--</hi>To his first and second prayer no answer came. To his third the answer came, which satisfied his faith and led him to bow his will to God's will. So Paul's master, Jesus, thrice prayed on the Mount of Olives, in resignation to the Father's will. The thorn seems (from <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.9">2Co 12:9</reference>, and Greek, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.7">2Co 12:7</reference>, "that he may buffet me") to have continued with Paul when he wrote, lest still he should be "overmuch lifted up."<div eID="gen34764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34765" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the Lord--</hi>Christ. Escape from the cross is not to be sought even indirectly from Satan (<reference osisRef="Luke.4.7">Lu 4:7</reference>). "Satan is not to be asked to spare us" [Bengel]. <div eID="gen34765" type="x-p"/>
entries.8c43e12b53338dab44b8ffa5151a86569d9772c9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17397"/><div sID="gen34766" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17397"/><hi type="bold">9. said--</hi>literally, "He hath said," implying that His answer is enough [Alford].<div eID="gen34766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34767" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is sufficient--</hi>The trial must endure, but the grace shall also endure and never fail thee [Alford], (<reference osisRef="Deut.33.25">De 33:25</reference>). The Lord puts the words into Paul's mouth, that following them up he might say, "O Lord, Thy grace is sufficient for me" [Bengel].<div eID="gen34767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34768" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my strength--</hi>Greek, "power."<div eID="gen34768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34769" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is made perfect--</hi>has its most perfect manifestation.<div eID="gen34769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34770" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in weakness--</hi>Do not ask for sensible strength, FOR My power is perfected in man's "strengthlessness" (so the Greek). The "for" implies, thy "strengthlessness" (the same Greek as is translated "weakness"; and in <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.10">2Co 12:10</reference>, "infirmities") is the very element in which My "power" (which moves coincident with "My grace") exhibits itself more perfectly. So that Paul instead of desiring the infirmity to "depart," "rather" henceforth "glories in infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest (Greek, 'tabernacle upon,' cover my infirmity all over as with a tabernacle; compare Greek, <reference osisRef="John.1.12">Joh 1:12</reference>) upon" him. This effect of Christ's assurance on him appears, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.7">2Co 4:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.3">1Co 2:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.4">4</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.14">1Pe 4:14</reference>. The "My" is omitted in some of the oldest manuscripts; the sense is the same, "power" (referring to God's power) standing absolutely, in contrast to "weakness" (put absolutely, for man's weakness). Paul often repeats the word "weakness" or "infirmity" (the eleventh, twelfth, and thirteenth chapters) as being Christ's own word. The Lord has more need of our weakness than of our strength: our strength is often His rival; our weakness, His servant, drawing on His resources, and showing forth His glory. Man's extremity is God's opportunity; man's security is Satan's opportunity. God's way is not to take His children out of trial, but to give them strength to bear up against it (<reference osisRef="Ps.88.7">Psa 88:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.17.15">Joh 17:15</reference>). <div eID="gen34770" type="x-p"/>
entries.e435b1ba22c8c73860a341e5a4c45d487cb7f7a1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17398"/><div sID="gen34771" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17398"/><hi type="bold">10. take pleasure in--</hi>too strongly. Rather as the Greek, "I am well contented in."<div eID="gen34771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34772" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">infirmities--</hi>the genus. Two pairs of species follow, partly coming from "Satan's messenger," partly from men.<div eID="gen34772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34773" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">reproaches--</hi>"insults."<div eID="gen34773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34774" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">when--</hi>in all the cases just specified.<div eID="gen34774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34775" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">then--</hi>then especially.<div eID="gen34775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34776" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">strong--</hi>"powerful" in "the power of Christ" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.12.9">2Co 12:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.13.4">2Co 13:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.11.34">He 11:34</reference>). <div eID="gen34776" type="x-p"/>
entries.d3ca336b55a46e83765e2e8a2e7014fc1cb685f9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17399"/><div sID="gen34777" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17399"/><hi type="bold">11. in glorying--</hi>omitted in the oldest manuscripts. "I am become a fool." He sounds a retreat [Bengel].<div eID="gen34777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34778" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye--</hi>emphatic. "It is YE who have compelled me; for I ought to have been commended by you," instead of having to commend myself.<div eID="gen34778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34779" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">am I behind--</hi>rather as Greek, "was I behind" when I was with you?<div eID="gen34779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34780" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the very chiefest--</hi>rather, as in <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.5">2Co 11:5</reference>, "those overmuch apostles."<div eID="gen34780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34781" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">though I be nothing--</hi>in myself (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.9">1Co 15:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.10">10</reference>). <div eID="gen34781" type="x-p"/>
entries.14105ef9dc326737a3d0df17528f88f655ea63cc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17400"/><div sID="gen34782" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17400"/><hi type="bold">12. Truly, &c.--</hi>There is understood some such clause as this, "And yet I have not been commended by you."<div eID="gen34782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34783" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in all patience, in signs, &c.--</hi>The oldest manuscripts omit "in." "Patience" is not one of the "signs," but the element IN which they were wrought: endurance of opposition which did not cause me to leave off working [Alford]. Translate, "In ... patience, BY signs," &c. His mode of expression is modest, putting himself, the worker, in the background, "were wrought," not "I wrought." As the signs have not been transmitted to us, neither has the apostleship. The apostles have no literal successors (compare <reference osisRef="Acts.1.21">Ac 1:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.22">22</reference>).<div eID="gen34783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34784" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mighty deeds--</hi>palpable works of divine omnipotence. The silence of the apostles in fourteen Epistles, as to miracles, arises from the design of those Epistles being hortatory, not controversial. The passing allusions to miracles in seven Epistles prove that the writers were not enthusiasts to whom miracles seem the most important thing. Doctrines were with them the important matter, save when convincing adversaries. In the seven Epistles the mention of miracles is not obtrusive, but marked by a calm air of assurance, as of facts acknowledged on all hands, and therefore unnecessary to dwell on. This is a much stronger proof of their reality than if they were formally and obtrusively asserted. Signs and wonders is the regular formula of the Old Testament, which New Testament readers would necessarily understand of supernatural works. Again, in the Gospels the miracles are so inseparably and congruously tied up with the history, that you cannot deny the former without denying the latter also. And then you have a greater difficulty than ever, namely, to account for the rise of Christianity; so that the infidel has something infinitely more difficult to believe than that which he rejects, and which the Christian more rationally accepts. <div eID="gen34784" type="x-p"/>
entries.0a0b2a3a5b08f7b7e619e3587335dbc20fcf9186: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17401"/><div sID="gen34785" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17401"/><hi type="bold">13. wherein you were inferior--</hi>that is, were treated with less consideration by me than were other churches.<div eID="gen34785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34786" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I myself--</hi>I made a gain of you neither myself, nor by those others whom I sent, Titus and others (<reference osisRef="2Cor.12.17">2Co 12:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.18">18</reference>).<div eID="gen34786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34787" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wrong--</hi>His declining support from the Corinthians might be regarded as the denial to them of a privilege, and a mark of their spiritual inferiority, and of his looking on them with less confidence and love (compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.9">2Co 11:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.11">11</reference>). <div eID="gen34787" type="x-p"/>
entries.c9d09fe9c3f87da1d6ca418846306b31046a7e1b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17402"/><div sID="gen34788" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17402"/><hi type="bold">14. the third time--</hi>See Introduction to the first Epistle. His second visit was probably a short one (<reference osisRef="1Cor.16.7">1Co 16:7</reference>), and attended with humiliation through the scandalous conduct of some of his converts (compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.21">2Co 12:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.1">2Co 2:1</reference>). It was probably paid during his three years' sojourn at Ephesus, from which he could pass so readily by sea to Corinth (compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.15">2Co 1:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.16">16</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.13.1">13:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.13.2">2</reference>). The context here implies nothing of a third preparation to come; but, "I am coming, and the third time, and will not burden you this time any more than I did at my two previous visits" [Alford].<div eID="gen34788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34789" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not yours, but you--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Phil.4.17">Php 4:17</reference>).<div eID="gen34789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34790" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">children ... parents--</hi>Paul was their spiritual father (<reference osisRef="1Cor.4.14">1Co 4:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.15">15</reference>). He does not, therefore, seek earthly treasure from them, but lays up the best treasure (namely, spiritual) "for their souls" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.12.15">2Co 12:15</reference>). <div eID="gen34790" type="x-p"/>
entries.04969463294678efdb2700138918cc23cb1584d4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17403"/><div sID="gen34791" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17403"/><hi type="bold">15. I will ... spend--</hi>all I have.<div eID="gen34791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34792" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">be spent--</hi>all that I am. This is more than even natural parents do. They "lay up treasures for their children." But I spend not merely my treasures, but myself.<div eID="gen34792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34793" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for you--</hi>Greek, "for your souls"; not for your mere bodies.<div eID="gen34793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34794" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the less I be loved--</hi>Love rather descends than ascends [Bengel]. Love him as a true friend who seeks your good more than your good will. <div eID="gen34794" type="x-p"/>
entries.24b376bdcc4d996a4f51ba0919534ae79f79acf0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17404"/><div sID="gen34795" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17404"/><hi type="bold">16. I did not burden you--</hi>The "I" in the Greek is emphatic. A possible insinuation of the Corinthians is hereby anticipated and refuted: "But, you may say, granted that I did not burden you myself; nevertheless, being crafty, I caught you (in my net) with guile"; namely, made a gain of you by means of others (<reference osisRef="1Thess.2.3">1Th 2:3</reference>). <div eID="gen34795" type="x-p"/>
entries.50333af9818a6bf2712ff4c09c9f9b99c9f1419f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17405"/><div sID="gen34796" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17405"/>17. Paul's reply: You know well I did not. My associates were as distinterested as myself. An important rule to all who would influence others for good. <div eID="gen34796" type="x-p"/>
entries.c6edebd5783dc79c37f1f0364645e1f693481c5c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17406"/><div sID="gen34797" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17406"/><hi type="bold">18. I desired Titus--</hi>namely, to go unto you. Not the mission mentioned <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.6">2Co 8:6</reference>, 17, 22; but a mission previous to this Epistle, probably that from which he had just returned announcing to Paul their penitence (<reference osisRef="2Cor.7.6-2Cor.7.16">2Co 7:6-16</reference>).<div eID="gen34797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34798" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a brother--</hi>rather "OUR (literally, 'the') brother"; one well known to the Corinthians, and perhaps a Corinthian; probably one of the two mentioned in <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.18">2Co 8:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.22">22</reference>.<div eID="gen34798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34799" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">same spirit--</hi>inwardly.<div eID="gen34799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34800" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">steps--</hi>outwardly. <div eID="gen34800" type="x-p"/>
entries.8924e6a41309cd618167a75fe6e02db05e2f8900: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17407"/><div sID="gen34801" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17407"/><hi type="bold">19. Again--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read, "This long time ye think that we are excusing ourselves unto you? (Nay). It is before God (as opposed to 'unto you') that we speak in Christ" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.2.17">2Co 2:17</reference>). English Version Greek text was a correction from <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.1">2Co 3:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.12">5:12</reference>. <div eID="gen34801" type="x-p"/>
entries.06a4025b23aca0da6c37040bebf18a720fedee56: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17408"/><div sID="gen34802" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17408"/><hi type="bold">20. For--</hi>Assigning cause why they needed to be thus spoken to "for their edification"; namely, his fear that at his coming he should find them "not such as he would," and so he should be found by them "such as they would not" like, namely, severe in punishing misconduct.<div eID="gen34802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34803" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">debates--</hi>Greek, "strifes," "contentions."<div eID="gen34803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34804" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">envyings--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read "envying," singular.<div eID="gen34804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34805" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">strifes--</hi>"factions," "intrigues," "factious schemes" [Wahl]. Ambitious self-seeking; from a Greek root, "to work for hire."<div eID="gen34805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34806" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">backbitings, whisperings--</hi>open "slanderings," and "whispering backbitings" (<reference osisRef="Gal.5.20">Ga 5:20</reference>).<div eID="gen34806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34807" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">swellings--</hi>arrogant elation; puffing up of yourselves. Jude 16, "great swelling words" (<reference osisRef="2Pet.2.18">2Pe 2:18</reference>). <div eID="gen34807" type="x-p"/>
entries.07b297839afb638157b0fe0f831a414aa39862a9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17409"/><div sID="gen34808" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17409"/><hi type="bold">21. my God--</hi>his God, however trying the humiliation that was in store for him.<div eID="gen34808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34809" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">will humble me--</hi>The indicative implies that the supposition will actually be so. The faithful pastor is "humbled" at, and "bewails" the falls of his people, as though they were his own.<div eID="gen34809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34810" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sinned already--</hi>before my last coming [Bengel], that is, before the second visit which he paid, and in which he had much at Corinth to rebuke.<div eID="gen34810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34811" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">have not repented--</hi>shall not have repented [Alford].<div eID="gen34811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34812" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">uncleanness--</hi>for example, of married persons (<reference osisRef="1Thess.4.7">1Th 4:7</reference>).<div eID="gen34812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34813" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fornication--</hi>among the unmarried. <chapter eID="2Cor.12"/>

entries.328f522892245e31a5c9f9c29e84d135ab4d59e3: <div eID="gen49419" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen49420" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen49421" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen49421" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen49420" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen49422" type="x-p"/> St. Paul mentions some wonderful revelations which he had received from the Lord, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.1-2Cor.12.5">2Cor 12:1-5</reference>. He speaks of his suffering in connection with these extraordinary revelations, that his character might be duly estimated, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.6">2Cor 12:6</reference>. That he might not be too much exalted, a messenger of Satan is sent to buffet him; his prayer for deliverance, and the Divine answer, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.7-2Cor.12.9">2Cor 12:7-9</reference>. He exults in sufferings and reproaches, and vindicates his apostleship, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.10-2Cor.12.13">2Cor 12:10-13</reference>. Promises to come and visit them, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.14">2Cor 12:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.15">2Cor 12:15</reference>. Answers some objections, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.16-2Cor.12.18">2Cor 12:16-18</reference>. And expresses his apprehensions that when he visits them he shall find many evils and disorders among them, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.19-2Cor.12.21">2Cor 12:19-21</reference>. <div eID="gen49422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49423" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen49423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49424" type="x-p"/> It is not expedient for me - There are several various readings on this verse which are too minute to be noticed here; they seem in effect to represent the verse thus: "If it be expedient to glory, (which does not become me), I will proceed to visions," etc. The plain meaning of the apostle, in this and the preceding chapter, in reference to glorying is, that though to boast in any attainments, or in what God did by him, was in all possible cases to be avoided, as being contrary to the humility and simplicity of the Gospel; yet the circumstances in which he was found, in reference to the Corinthian Church, and his detractors there, rendered it absolutely necessary; not for his personal vindication, but for the honor of the Gospel, the credit of which was certainly at stake. <div eID="gen49424" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49425" type="x-p"/> I will come to visions - Οπτασιας· Symbolical representations of spiritual and celestial things, in which matters of the deepest importance are exhibited to the eye of the mind by a variety of emblems, the nature and properties of which serve to illustrate those spiritual things. <div eID="gen49425" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49426" type="x-p"/> Revelations - Αποκαλυψεις· A manifestation of things not before known, and such as God alone can make known, because they are a part of his own inscrutable counsels.
entries.bcebe637d70a0944a11ce8bc830862e8cfdb2d85: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen49426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49427" type="x-p"/> I knew a man in Christ - I knew a Christian, or a Christian man; for to such alone God now revealed himself, for vision and prophecy had been shut up from the Jews. <div eID="gen49427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49428" type="x-p"/> Fourteen years ago - On what occasion or in what place this transaction took place we cannot tell; there are many conjectures among learned men concerning it, but of what utility can they be when every thing is so palpably uncertain? Allowing this epistle to have been written some time in the year 57, fourteen years counted backward will lead this transaction to the year 42 or 43, which was about the time that Barnabas brought Paul from Tarsus to Antioch, <reference osisRef="Act.11.25">Act 11:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Act.11.26">Act 11:26</reference>, and when he and Paul were sent by the Church of Antioch with alms to the poor Christians at Jerusalem. It is very possible that, on this journey, or while in Jerusalem, he had this vision, which was intended to be the means of establishing him in the faith, and supporting him in the many trials and difficulties through which he was to pass. This vision the apostle had kept secret for fourteen years. <div eID="gen49428" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49429" type="x-p"/> Whether in the body I cannot tell - That the apostle was in an ecstasy or trance, something like that of Peter, <reference osisRef="Act.10.9">Act 10:9</reference>, etc., there is reason to believe; but we know that being carried literally into heaven was possible to the Almighty. But as he could not decide himself, it would be ridiculous in us to attempt it. <div eID="gen49429" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49430" type="x-p"/> Caught up to the third heaven - He appeared to have been carried up to this place; but whether bodily he could not tell, or whether the spirit were not separated for the time, and taken up to the third heaven, he could not tell. <div eID="gen49430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49431" type="x-p"/> The third heaven - The Jews talk of seven heavens, and Mohammed has received the same from them; but these are not only fabulous but absurd. I shall enumerate those of the Jews. <div eID="gen49431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49432" type="x-p"/> 1. The Velum, or curtain, וילון - "Which in the morning is folded up, and in the evening stretched out." <reference osisRef="Isa.40.22">Isa 40:22</reference> : He stretcheth out the heavens as a Curtain, and spreadeth them out as a tent to dwell in. <div eID="gen49432" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49433" type="x-p"/> 2. The firmament, or Expanse, רקיע - "In which the sun, moon, stars, and constellations are fixed." <reference osisRef="Gen.1.17">Gen 1:17</reference> : And God placed them in the Firmament of heaven. <div eID="gen49433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49434" type="x-p"/> 3. The Clouds, or Ether, שקים - "Where the mill-stones are which grind the manna for the righteous." <reference osisRef="Psa.78.23">Psa 78:23</reference>, etc.: Though he had commended the Clouds from above, and opened the doors of heaven, and had rained down manna, etc. <div eID="gen49434" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49435" type="x-p"/> 4. The Habitation, זבול - "Where Jerusalem, and the temple, and the altar, were constructed and where Michael the great prince stands and offers sacrifices." <reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.13">1Kgs 8:13</reference> : I have surely built thee a House To Dwell In, a settled place for thee to abide in for ever. "But where is heaven so called?" Answer: In <reference osisRef="Isa.63.15">Isa 63:15</reference> : Look down from Heaven, and behold from the Habitation, מזבול, of thy holiness. <div eID="gen49435" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49436" type="x-p"/> 5. The Dwelling-Place, מעון - "Where the troops of angels sing throughout the night, but are silent in the day time, because of the glory of the Israelites." <reference osisRef="Psa.42.8">Psa 42:8</reference> : The Lord will command his loving-kindness in the day time, and in the night his song shall be with me. "But how is it proved that this means heaven? "Answer: From <reference osisRef="Deu.26.15">Deu 26:15</reference>. Look down from thy holy habitation, ממעון, the Dwelling-Place of thy holiness; and from heaven, השמים, and bless thy people Israel. <div eID="gen49436" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49437" type="x-p"/> 6. The Fixed Residence, מבון - "Where are the treasures of snow and hail, the repository of noxious dews, of drops, and whirlwinds; the grotto of exhalations," etc. "But where are the heavens thus denominated?" Answer: In <reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.39">1Kgs 8:39</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.49">1Kgs 8:49</reference>, etc.: Then hear thou in Heaven thy Dwelling - Place, מכון שבת, thy Fixed Residence. <div eID="gen49437" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49438" type="x-p"/> 7. The Araboth, ערבות - "Where are justice, judgment, mercy, the treasures of life; peace and blessedness; the souls of the righteous, the souls and spirits which are reserved for the bodies yet to be formed, and the dew by which God is to vivify the dead." <reference osisRef="Psa.89.14">Psa 89:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.59.17">Isa 59:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Psa.36.9">Psa 36:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jdg.6.24">Jdg 6:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Psa.24.4">Psa 24:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.29">1Sam 25:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.57.20">Isa 57:20</reference> : All of which are termed Araboth, <reference osisRef="Psa.68.4">Psa 68:4</reference>. Extol him who rideth on the heavens, בערבות ba Araboth, by his name Jah. <div eID="gen49438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49439" type="x-p"/> All this is sufficiently unphilosophical, and in several cases ridiculous. <div eID="gen49439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49440" type="x-p"/> In the sacred writings three heavens only are mentioned. The first is the atmosphere, what appears to be intended by רקיע rekia, the firmament or expansion, <reference osisRef="Gen.1.6">Gen 1:6</reference>. The second, the starry heaven; where are the sun, moon, planets, and stars; but these two are often expressed under the one term שמים shamayim, the two heavens, or expansions, and in <reference osisRef="Gen.1.17">Gen 1:17</reference>, they appear to be both expressed by רקיע השמים rekia hashshamayim, the firmament of heaven. And, thirdly, the place of the blessed, or the throne of the Divine glory, probably expressed by the words שמי השמים shemei hashshamayim, the heavens of heavens. But on these subjects the Scripture affords us but little light; and on this distinction the reader is not desired to rely. <div eID="gen49440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49441" type="x-p"/> Much more may be seen in Schoettgen, who has exhausted the subject; and who has shown that ascending to heaven, or being caught up to heaven, is a form of speech among the Jewish writers to express the highest degrees of inspiration. They often say of Moses that he ascended on high, ascended on the firmament, ascended to heaven; where it is evident they mean only by it that he was favored with the nearest intimacy with God, and the highest revelations relative to his will, etc. If we may understand St. Paul thus, it will remove much of the difficulty from this place; and perhaps the unspeakable words, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.4">2Cor 12:4</reference>, are thus to be understood. He had the most sublime communications from God, such as would be improper to mention, though it is very likely that we have the substance of these in his epistles. Indeed, the two epistles before us seem, in many places, to be the effect of most extraordinary revelations.
entries.4c11ff12bc7cda61f82008196b43b21265c59531: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen49441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49442" type="x-p"/> Caught up into paradise - The Jewish writers have no less than four paradises, as they have seven heavens; but it is needless to wade through their fables. On the word paradise see the note on <reference osisRef="Gen.2.8">Gen 2:8</reference>. The Mohammedans call it jennet alferdoos, the garden of paradise, and say that God created it out of light, and that it is the habitation of the prophets and wise men. <div eID="gen49442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49443" type="x-p"/> Among Christian writers it generally means the place of the blessed, or the state of separate spirits. Whether the third heaven and paradise be the same place we cannot absolutely say; they probably are not; and it is likely that St. Paul, at the time referred to, had at least two of these raptures. <div eID="gen49443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49444" type="x-p"/> Which it is not lawful for a man to utter - The Jews thought that the Divine name, the Tetragrammaton יהוה Yehovah, should not be uttered, and that it is absolutely unlawful to pronounce it; indeed they say that the true pronunciation is utterly lost, and cannot be recovered without an express revelation. Not one of them, to the present day, ever attempts to utter it; and, when they meet with it in their reading, always supply its place with אדני Adonai, Lord. It is probable that the apostle refers to some communication concerning the Divine nature and the Divine economy, of which he was only to make a general use in his preaching and writing. No doubt that what he learned at this time formed the basis of all his doctrines. <div eID="gen49444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49445" type="x-p"/> Cicero terms God illud inexprimible, that inexpressible Being. And Hermes calls him ανεκλαλητος, αρῥητος, σιωπῃ φωνουμενος· The ineffable, the unspeakable, and that which is to be pronounced in silence. We cannot have views too exalted of the majesty of God; and the less frequently we pronounce his name, the more reverence shall we feel for his nature. It is said of Mr. Boyle that he never pronounced the name of God without either taking off his hat or making a bow. Leaving out profane swearers, blasphemers, and such like open-faced servants of Satan, it is distressing to hear many well intentioned people making unscripturally free with this sacred name.
entries.208568ef66ffa8fd0de38e7c21f14e69af28b39d: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen49445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49446" type="x-p"/> Of such a one will I glory - Through modesty he does not mention himself, though the account can be understood of no other person; for, did he mean any other, the whole account would be completely irrelevant.
entries.060768f0aed756f989aa9767d41f672e246d129a: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen49446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49447" type="x-p"/> I shall not be a fool - Who that had got such honor from God would have been fourteen years silent on the subject? <div eID="gen49447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49448" type="x-p"/> I will say the truth - I speak nothing but truth; and the apostle seems to have intended to proceed with something else of the same kind, but, finding some reason probably occurring suddenly, says, I forbear - I will say no more on this subject. <div eID="gen49448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49449" type="x-p"/> Lest any man should think of me above - The apostle spoke of these revelations for two purposes: first, lest his enemies might suppose they had cause to think meanly of him; and, secondly, having said thus much, he forbears to speak any farther of them, lest his friends should think too highly of him. It is a rare gift to discern when to speak, and when to be silent; and to know when enough is said on a subject, neither too little nor too much.
entries.b9e124aa558d120f2678857af4ac37540c84a8b5: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen49449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49450" type="x-p"/> And lest I should be exalted - There were three evils to be guarded against: <div eID="gen49450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49451" type="x-p"/> 1. The contempt of his gifts and call by his enemies. <div eID="gen49451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49452" type="x-p"/> 2. The overweening fondness of his friends. And, Self-exultation. <div eID="gen49452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49453" type="x-p"/> A thorn in the flesh - The word σκολοψ signifies a stake, and ανασκολοπιζεσθαι, to be tied to a stake by way of punishment; and it is used, says Schoettgen, to signify the most oppressive afflictions. Whatever it was, it was τῃ σαρκι, in the flesh, i.e. of an outward kind. It was neither sin nor sinfulness, for this could not be given him to prevent his being exalted above measure; for sin never had and never can have this tendency. What this thorn in the flesh might be has given birth to a multitude of conjectures: Tertullian thought it dolor auriculae, the ear ache; Chrysostom, κεφαλαλγια, the head ache; Cyprian, carnis et corporis multa ac gravia tormenta, many and grievous bodily torments. I believe the apostle to refer simply to the distresses he had endured through the opposition he met with at Corinth; which were as painful and grievous to him as a thorn in his flesh, or his being bound to a stake; for, if he could have devoted himself to destruction, <reference osisRef="Rom.9.3">Rom 9:3</reference>, for his rebellious and unbelieving countrymen, what must he have suffered on account of an eminent Church being perverted and torn to pieces by a false teacher! God permitted this to keep the apostle humble, and at last completely delivered the Church out of the hands and influence of this deceiver; none, not even the incestuous person, having been turned finally out of the way by the false doctrines there preached. <div eID="gen49453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49454" type="x-p"/> The messenger of Satan - Another mode of expressing what he calls the thorn in the flesh; and he seems most plainly to refer to the false apostle at Corinth. The apostle himself was, as he styles himself to this Church, αποστολος Ιησου Χριστου, <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.1">2Cor 1:1</reference>, the apostle of Jesus Christ. The person in question is styled here αγγελος Σαταν, the apostle or angel of Satan. It is almost impossible to mistake the apostle's meaning and reference. Jesus Christ sent Paul to proclaim his truth, and found a Church at Corinth. Satan, the adversary of God's truth, sent a man to preach lies at the same place, and turn the Church of God into his own synagogue; and by his teaching lies and calumnies the apostle was severely buffeted. We need seek no other sense for these expressions. Many, however, think that the apostle had really some bodily infirmity that rendered him contemptible, and was the means of obstructing the success of his ministry; and that the false apostle availed himself of this to set St. Paul at nought, and to hold him out to ridicule. I have shown this, elsewhere, to be very unlikely. <div eID="gen49454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49455" type="x-p"/> The best arguments in favor of this opinion may be found in Whitby; but I forbear to transcribe them because I think the meaning given above is more correct. No infirmity of body nor corporeal sufferings can affect and distress a minister of the Gospel, equally to the perversion or scattering of a flock, which were the fruit of innumerable labors, watchings, fastings, prayers, and tears.
entries.8366e6d27ae95ee04839d6c3972238d52bf61e83: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen49455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49456" type="x-p"/> I besought the Lord - That is, Christ, as the next verse absolutely proves, and the Socinians themselves confess. And if Christ be an object of prayer in such a case as this, or indeed in any case, it is a sure proof of his divinity; for only an omniscient Being can be made an object of prayer. <div eID="gen49456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49457" type="x-p"/> Thrice - Several suppose this to be a certain number for an uncertain; as if he had said, I often besought Christ to deliver me from this tormentor: or, which is perhaps more likely, the apostle may refer to three solemn, fixed, and fervent applications made to Christ at different times; at the last of which he received the answer which he immediately subjoins. It is worthy of remark, that our Lord in his agony acted in the same way: at three different times he applied to God that the cup might depart from him; and in each application he spoke the same words, <reference osisRef="Mat.26.39-Mat.26.44">Mat 26:39-44</reference>. There is, therefore, a manifest allusion to our Lord's conduct in these words of the apostle.
entries.a6d453ffb985b7e667e0487fe273fac144c2cff6: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen49457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49458" type="x-p"/> My grace is sufficient for thee - Thou shalt not be permitted to sink under these afflictions. Thy enemies shall not be able to prevail against thee. <div eID="gen49458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49459" type="x-p"/> My strength is made perfect in weakness - The more, and the more violently, thou art afflicted and tried, being upheld by my power, and prospered in all thy labors, the more eminently will my power be seen and acknowledged. For the weaker the instrument I use, the more the power of my grace shall be manifested. See at the end of this chapter, (<reference osisRef="2Cor.12.21">2Cor 12:21</reference> (note)). <div eID="gen49459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49460" type="x-p"/> Will I rather glory in my infirmities - Therefore, his infirmities do not mean his corruptions, or sins, or sinfulness of any kind; for it would be blasphemous for any man to say, I will rather glory that God leaves my corruptions in me, than that he should take them away. <div eID="gen49460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49461" type="x-p"/> That the power of Christ may rest upon me - Επισκηνωσῃ επ' εμε· That it may overshadow me as a tent, or tabernacle; affording me shelter, protection, safety, and rest. This expression is like that, <reference osisRef="Joh.1.14">Joh 1:14</reference> : And the word was made flesh, και εσκηνωσεν εν ἡμιν and made his tabernacle among us - full of grace and truth. The same eternal Word promised to make his tabernacle with the apostle, and gives him a proof that he was still the same - full of grace and truth, by assuring him that his grace should be sufficient for him. Paul, knowing that the promise of grace could not fail, because of the Divine truth, says: Most gladly, therefore, will I rather glory in my afflictions, that such a power of Christ may overshadow and defend me. <div eID="gen49461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49462" type="x-p"/> The words are also similar to those of the Prophet Isaiah, <reference osisRef="Isa.4.5">Isa 4:5</reference> : On all the glory shall be a defense. God gives the glory, and God gives the defense of that glory. The apostle had much glory or honor; both Satan and his apostles were very envious; in himself the apostle, as well as all human beings, was weak, and therefore needed the power of God to defend such glory. Grace alone can preserve grace. When we get a particular blessing we need another to preserve it; and without this we shall soon be shorn of our strength, and become as other men. Hence the necessity of continual watchfulness and prayer, and depending on the all-sufficient grace of Christ. See on <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.30">2Cor 11:30</reference> (note)
entries.c52338fab4376eac28150ccff28e4313f16f46a7: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen49462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49463" type="x-p"/> Therefore I take pleasure - I not only endure them patiently, but am pleased when they occur; for I do it for Christ's sake - on his account; for on his account I suffer. For when I am weak - most oppressed with trials and afflictions, then am I strong; God supporting my mind with his most powerful influences, causing me to rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory.
entries.a41d2d00678da64f4ceb1b1bfb7e517d2591b022: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen49463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49464" type="x-p"/> I am become a fool in glorying - It is not the part of a wise or gracious man to boast; but ye have compelled me - I have been obliged to do it, in order to vindicate the cause of God. <div eID="gen49464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49465" type="x-p"/> I ought to have been commended of you - You should have vindicated both myself and my ministry against the detractors that are among you. <div eID="gen49465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49466" type="x-p"/> The very chiefest apostles - See <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.1">2Cor 11:1</reference>. <div eID="gen49466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49467" type="x-p"/> Though I be nothing - Though I have been thus set at nought by your false apostle; and though, in consequence of what he has said, some of you have been ready to consider me as nothing - what we call good for nothing. This must be the meaning of the apostle, as the following verses prove. <div eID="gen49467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49468" type="x-p"/> A kind of technical meaning has been imposed on these words, of which many good people seem very fond. I am nothing - I am all sin, defilement, and unworthiness in myself; but Jesus Christ is all in all. This latter clause is an eternal truth; the former may be very true also; the person who uses it may be all sin, defilement, etc., but let him not say that the apostle of the Gentiles was so too, because this is not true; it is false, and it is injurious to the character of the apostle and to the grace of Christ; besides, it is not the meaning of the text, and the use commonly made of it is abominable, if not wicked.
entries.cd7875de6f8814b800fe98c8648206fcb9ca47a7: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen49468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49469" type="x-p"/> The signs of an apostle were wrought among you - Though I have been reputed as nothing, I have given the fullest proof of my Divine mission by various signs, wonders, and miracles, and by that patience which I have manifested towards you: though I had power from God to inflict punishment on the transgressors, I have in every case forborne to do it. Is the man nothing who wrought such miracles among you?
entries.c381d02ccfb7ad442486e84d369742a54ca90a41: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen49469" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49470" type="x-p"/> For what is it wherein you were inferior - This is a fine, forcible, yet delicate stroke. It was your duty and your interest to have supported your apostle; other Churches have done so: I did not require this from you; in this respect all other Churches are superior to you. I am the cause of your inferiority, by not giving you an opportunity of ministering to my necessities: forgive me the wrong I have done you. It is the privilege of the Churches of Christ to support the ministry of his Gospel among them. Those who do not contribute their part to the support of the Gospel ministry either care nothing for it, or derive no good from it.
entries.fdeeac09a30b02e68413c72f07fb3742f4acd009: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen49470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49471" type="x-p"/> The third time I am ready - That is, this is the third time that I am ready - have formed the resolution, to visit you. He had formed this resolution twice before, but was disappointed. See <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.5">1Cor 16:5</reference>, and <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.15">2Cor 1:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.16">2Cor 1:16</reference>. He now formed it a third time, having more probability of seeing them now than he had before. See <reference osisRef="2Cor.13.2">2Cor 13:2</reference>. <div eID="gen49471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49472" type="x-p"/> I seek not yours, but you - I seek your salvation, I desire not your property; others have sought your property, but not your salvation. See <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.20">2Cor 11:20</reference>. <div eID="gen49472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49473" type="x-p"/> For the children ought not to lay up for the parents - You may have many teachers, but you have but one Father; for in Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the Gospel; see <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.15">1Cor 4:15</reference>. Ye are my children, and I am your father. You have not contributed to my support, but I have been labouring for your life. I will act towards you as the loving father who works hard, and lays up what is necessary to enable his children to get their bread.
entries.dfe5a9d0d89c46905cc18b5e5d3703dcd63aed40: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen49473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49474" type="x-p"/> And I will very gladly spend and be spent for you - I will continue to act as a loving father, who spends all he has upon his children, and expends his own strength and life in providing for them the things necessary for their preservation and comfort. <div eID="gen49474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49475" type="x-p"/> Though the more abundantly I love you - I will even act towards you with the most affectionate tenderness, though it happen to me, as it often does to loving fathers, that their disobedient children love them less, in proportion as their love to them is increased. Does it not frequently happen that the most disobedient child in the family is that one on which the parents' tenderness is more especially placed? See the parable of the prodigal son.
